chapter: Probation, Las Vegas and Los Angeles in the 1950s
title: Back in Los Angeles in 1953: no jobs, the merged union and the Lighthouse
summary: Old colleagues were out of music; he sat in at Howard Rumsey's Lighthouse.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: So did you play out here then?

No, because all of the groups were organized and all the fellows that I had played with prior to my leaving California wasn't playing music anymore. They were in the Post Office, or they was running on the road, on the trains, or they had retired or something. They had departed, or something had happened to them, and they weren't playing music anymore. So the youngsters out here, they didn't know anything about me, me spending all of my time in New York, you know. So I was just another musician as far as they were concerned. And at that time, the union had just merged and they had a party over at the old Florentine Gardens for the merger.
Uh-huh. On Hollywood Boulevard.

Yes. And I ran into a couple of my old cronies. Red Calendar was over there with Jerry Fielding. He played, you know. Different bands got up and played, you know. And I said, 'Well, this looks all right.' So I joined the union, but I didn't get any jobs, because I didn't know anyone, you know, other than the fellows who were appearing down at the Lighthouse, and that was already organized. They had their men down there, you know, that was, how do you say it? Enconced? Is that the word?
Enseanced.
Well, it was Howard Rumsey's gig anyway, wasn't it? As far as bass playing went.

Yeah. But he stayed there so long, though, that everyone was under the impression that the club belonged to him, because he built it up, and he had behind his name being used, Howard Rumsey's Lighthouse by the Sea.
And Howard Rumsey's Lighthouse All Stars. Nobody ever mentioned that John Levine owned the club.

No. So I'd go out there and sit in. Howard would be glad to see me come, and let me sit in in his place, you know, and he'd get out and mingle with the audience, the public, you know. And at that time they had Bob Cooper and Stanley --
Frank Rosolino and Conte Condoli, were they playing out there?
No, they weren't there then. Was it Williamson?
Claude?
Yeah.
Or Stu?
The trumpet player.
Stu. (Williamson)
Stu. He was there. And the pianist, I think, was Russ Freeman, if I'm not mistaken.
Shelly played out there sometimes, didn't he?

Later. But I mean when I first got back there he wasn't out there. So I think Shelly took Stan's place, because Stan went into the photography business. You know, he stopped playing music. He found out he could make more money as a photographer.
He's a good photographer.
